COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Artist — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace ARTIST, match the artist to the paintbrush, the palette and the easel, circle the art supplies, count the paintbrushes and draw a picture that is all your own.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

← Animal Shelter WorkerPrevious activityDelivery Driver →Next activity
HOW TO DO IT

Five little steps.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word ARTIST across the row — six letters, one for every color of the rainbow.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the artist to the paintbrush, the palette and the easel.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every art supply. Friendly news: every single one belongs in the artist’s studio!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the paintbrushes, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a picture that is all your own in the big box — anything at all; this is YOUR gallery wall.

Ask a grown-up to read the steps aloud the first time. After that, you know just what to do.

YOUR PENCIL CASE

Pick your tools.

Pencil, nine crayons, an eraser, undo, redo and clear — the tools appear right here and work on the sheet. Save keeps your finished work as a picture, and your saved work comes back next time.

MY PROGRESS

Save it to keep it.

This activity is cleared for you the moment you save your finished sheet. Nothing counts until then — opening the page is just opening the door.

Cleared! Your saved work for this sheet is in your downloads, and the ribbon is on in Class 33.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What an artist does all day, what the palette and easel are for, and which tools make pictures happen — plus how to write the word ARTIST.

Knowledge to have ready: An artist makes pictures and sculptures from ideas: the paintbrush carries the color, the palette holds every color side by side, and the easel stands the canvas up tall. Pencils, markers, glue and scissors are artists’ helpers too — the whole grid is on the artist’s side!

Why this activity matters: Every child is already an artist; this sheet simply names the tools and hands over the permission. The all-friendly grid builds sorting confidence, and the final draw box is deliberately empty — the sheet ends by asking your child to be the artist.

  • Art vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Supply sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Free drawing

What to say before you start: "This is an artist — the maker of beautiful pictures. Trace the name, then connect the paintbrush, the palette and the easel. Now the six pictures: every one is an art supply! Circle them all. Count the paintbrushes slowly, and then the big box is yours — draw whatever YOU love."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the palette and count the colors sitting on it. In the grid, name each supply and ask what it makes: marks, lines, sticking or snipping. In the draw box, stay quiet and nearby; when it is done, ask what is happening in the picture rather than what it is.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the artist hold on the palette?" "Which supplies did you circle — which have YOU used?" "Where does an artist get ideas?" "Tell me about your drawing — what is happening in it?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: No tricks in this grid — pencils, markers, glue and scissors are all studio friends, so circle every one with confidence. For the big draw box there is no wrong answer: start with one line and see where it walks.

Parent tips: Display the finished drawing like a real gallery — a fridge frame and a title card written by the artist. Name real artists your child knows: the aunt who paints, the illustrator inside a favorite book. Art is a job made of play.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who makes pictures for a living? Name two art supplies from the grid. How many paintbrushes?" The artist, two supplies, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Set up a two-minute studio tonight: paper, two colors, one brush — and let your child be the artist while you are the assistant who rinses the brushes. Ask for the picture’s story, not its accuracy.

This activity belongs to Class 33 — Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood on the Learning Path. Progress is saved on this device for the child chosen in My Classroom — and only a real save of finished work marks it cleared, never just opening the page.
